title: Comparing themes across texts
blurb: State a theme as a full message about life, then find the theme two different texts share and how they treat it differently.
question: A TEAS item pairs a short story about a widow whose neighbors help her clean up after a flood with a news report on volunteers who rebuilt a town library. One option says both texts share the theme 'floods.' Another says 'neighbors can help people recover from hardship.' Which is the theme, and why is the other wrong?

teach.h: Theme: the message beneath the story
teach.body: Formally, a theme is the central message, lesson or insight about life or human nature that a text expresses. It is usually implied, not stated, and it is written as a complete statement, such as 'Perseverance can overcome hardship.' In plain English: the topic is what the text is about (perseverance); the theme is what the text says about it. If your answer is one word, you have found the topic, not the theme.

teach.caption: A theme applies beyond this one story. A plot summary is tied to its characters and events.

teach.body:
Text A (story): When the river crested, Ruth, seventy-two, watched mud swallow her kitchen. She had told no one she needed help. By morning, six neighbors stood at her door with shovels. 'You fed our kids for thirty years,' one said. 'Our turn.'

Text B (news report): Six weeks after the flood, the Dalton Public Library reopened. More than 200 residents, some of whom had lost their own homes, volunteered to dry books, paint walls and rebuild shelves.

teach.h: Finding a theme in four moves
items: Name the conflict or problem (a flood damages homes and a library).
Notice how people respond or change (neighbors and residents step in to help).
Ask what lesson that response teaches about life, beyond these people.
Write it as a complete, general sentence with no character names: 'Communities help people recover from hardship.'

head: Topic (one word)
Theme (full statement)
rows: Greed can cost people what matters most.
Accepting who you are brings peace.
People are stronger when they help each other.
Progress can come at nature's expense.
teach.caption: One topic can carry many different themes, so always test the statement against the text.

teach.body: To compare is to find similarities; to contrast is to find differences. With two texts, first find the theme or central idea both share, then ask how they differ: genre, purpose, tone or evidence. Text A is a story told through one woman's experience; Text B is a news report using numbers. Different genres, same theme. In informational pairs, compare central ideas, claims, approaches, purposes, evidence and conclusions.

teach.text: Four theme traps: a one-word answer (that is a topic), a plot summary with names, a theme that fits only ONE of the two texts when the question asks for both, and a shared minor detail (both mention mud) chosen over the shared central idea. Also, different tones do not mean the authors disagree.

teach.body: Mei Lin, applying to a radiography program, is asked which theme both flood texts share. 'Natural disasters' is a topic. 'Ruth's neighbors repay her kindness' is a plot summary that fits only Text A. 'Libraries are important to towns' fits only Text B. 'People find strength in their community after a disaster' fits both texts and is a complete, general statement, so she chooses it.

items: Theme = a message about life, stated as a complete general sentence.
A single word is a topic; a sentence with names and events is a plot summary.
A shared theme must fit BOTH texts, even across different genres.
Different tones do not mean the authors disagree about the theme.

summary: You can now state a theme as a complete message about life and tell it apart from a topic or a plot summary. You can also find the theme two texts share and describe how they develop it differently.

A.q:
Read the passage.

Every afternoon for a month, Jaden practiced free throws in the empty school gym after his teammates went home. He missed far more than he made at first, and twice he nearly quit. At the final game of the season, with two seconds left, he sank both shots to win.

Which statement best expresses the theme of the passage?
options: Practicing free throws in an empty school gym
Jaden wins the final game with two free throws.
Steady effort can lead to success under pressure.
Teammates should practice together after school.
A.why: A theme is a general message about life. Jaden's lonely, persistent practice paying off when it counts expresses that steady effort leads to success under pressure.

whyNot.0: This is a topic: a phrase with no message about life.
whyNot.1: This is a plot summary tied to one character and event, not a general lesson.
whyNot.3: The passage shows Jaden practicing alone; this recommendation is not its message.

A.q:
Read the poem.

The oak outside my window
lost a limb in last year's storm.
This spring it pushed out new green leaves
along the broken arm.

Which theme does the poem most clearly express?
options: Storms cause serious damage to trees each spring.
People should protect trees from heavy storms.
Old oak trees are stronger than younger trees.
Life can renew itself after it has been damaged.
A.why: The broken oak grows new leaves on the damaged limb: an image of renewal after harm, which is the poem's message about life.

whyNot.0: The storm was last year, and the poem's focus is the new growth, not the damage.
whyNot.1: The poem gives no advice about protecting trees.
whyNot.2: The poem compares the oak with no other trees.

A.q:
Read the two texts.

Text 1: After Aisha's family moved from Somalia to Minnesota, she spoke only to her little brother at school for months. Then the school nurse asked Aisha to help a new student who spoke only Somali. Translating for him, Aisha heard her own voice grow confident.

Text 2: A study of first-year college students found that those who tutored other students reported feeling more at home on campus than those who did not.

Which idea do both texts share?
options: Moving to a new country is hardest for younger children.
College students learn best when tutored by their peers.
Helping others can build a person's sense of belonging.
Schools should hire more translators for new students.
A.why: Aisha gains confidence by helping a new student, and the tutors in the study feel more at home on campus. Both show helping others building belonging.

whyNot.0: This relates to Text 1's setting but is not its message, and Text 2 is about college students.
whyNot.1: Text 2 is about the tutors' feelings, not how tutored students learn; Text 1 is not about college.
whyNot.3: Neither text recommends hiring; this is a policy idea neither author makes.

B.q:
Read the two texts.

Text 1: Grandpa Leo kept every receipt for forty years and could tell you what bread cost in 1985. When he died, his children found he had quietly paid for three neighbors' kids to go to college.

Text 2: Tamsin bought the newest phone every year and posted each one online. When her car broke down, she had no savings, and none of her online followers offered to help.

Which theme fits Text 1 but NOT Text 2?
options: Spending habits can reveal what a person values.
Careful saving can let a person give generously.
Possessions can matter more than relationships.
Money troubles can arrive without much warning.
B.why: Leo's careful habits allowed his hidden generosity. Text 2 shows the opposite: spending left Tamsin with nothing to give or fall back on.

whyNot.0: This fits BOTH texts: Leo's thrift and Tamsin's spending each show what they value.
whyNot.2: This fits Text 2 more than Text 1; Leo chose people over things.
whyNot.3: This fits Text 2 (the car breakdown) but not Text 1.

B.q:
Read the two texts.

Text 1 (memoir): The first time I drew blood as a phlebotomy student, my hands shook so badly my instructor had to steady them. By my hundredth draw, patients asked for me by name.

Text 2 (article): Researchers who study skill learning report that most beginners improve fastest through many short practice sessions with feedback.

How do the two texts differ in the way they present their shared idea?
options: Text 1 uses personal experience; Text 2 uses research.
Text 1 argues for more practice; Text 2 argues against it.
Text 1 is about medicine; Text 2 is about sports skills.
Text 1 is neutral in tone; Text 2 is openly emotional.
B.why: Both show skill growing through practice. The memoir makes the point through one person's story, while the article reports research findings: a difference in genre and evidence.

whyNot.1: Both texts support practice; they do not disagree.
whyNot.2: Text 2 never mentions sports; it discusses skill learning in general.
whyNot.3: This reverses the tones: the memoir is personal and the article is neutral.

B.q:
Read the two texts.

Text 1: The Greenway Clinic cut wait times by letting patients check in by text, which freed staff to spend more time with patients.

Text 2: A rural pharmacy began mailing refills, so its two pharmacists could hold longer counseling sessions in the store.

Which central idea do both texts share?
options: Rural patients wait longer than city patients for care.
Text messages are the best way to contact patients.
Pharmacists need more training in counseling patients.
Simple changes can give staff more time with patients.
B.why: In both texts, a simple process change (text check-in, mailed refills) frees staff to spend more time with patients.

whyNot.0: Neither text compares rural and city wait times.
whyNot.1: Only Text 1 mentions texting, and neither calls it the best method.
whyNot.2: Neither text discusses training; Text 2 is about time for counseling.

C.q:
Read the two texts.

Text 1 (poem):
My mother's hands, cracked from bleach,
scrubbed hospital floors at night
so mine could hold these textbooks
under library light.

Text 2 (essay): Many first-generation college students describe a debt they can never fully repay: parents who worked long, hard jobs so their children could study.

Which statement best describes how the texts relate?
options: Both express gratitude for a parent's sacrifice for a child's education.
Both argue that hospital cleaning jobs should pay workers much more.
Text 1 celebrates the parent's work; Text 2 says the debt is a burden.
Text 1 is about one family; Text 2 says few families sacrifice this way.
C.why: The poem shows one mother's hard work making the speaker's study possible; the essay describes many students feeling that same debt. Different genres, same theme of gratitude for sacrifice.

whyNot.1: Neither text discusses pay; the hospital job is a detail in the poem.
whyNot.2: The essay's 'debt' is gratitude, not a complaint; the texts do not disagree.
whyNot.3: The essay says 'many' students describe this, not that it is rare.

C.q:
Read the two texts.

Text 1: Honestly, who has time for breakfast? Me, now. After years of grabbing coffee and crashing by ten, I started eating eggs and fruit at seven, and my mornings stopped feeling like a cliff.

Text 2: In a survey of 400 office workers, those who ate breakfast reported higher energy before noon than those who skipped it.

A student says the authors disagree because Text 1 is casual and Text 2 is formal. Why is the student mistaken?
options: Both texts link eating breakfast to better morning energy.
Text 2 uses a survey, and surveys outweigh personal stories.
Text 1 is also formal, since it describes a daily schedule.
Both texts urge readers to stop drinking coffee each morning.
C.why: A difference in tone is not a disagreement. The casual writer and the formal survey both connect eating breakfast with better energy before midday.

whyNot.1: This may be true about evidence strength, but it does not address whether the authors disagree.
whyNot.2: Text 1's chatty style ('Honestly, who has time...') is clearly informal.
whyNot.3: Neither text tells readers to stop drinking coffee.

C.q:
Read the two texts.

Text 1: In the fable, a crow too proud to ask the other birds where water could be found flew alone until it collapsed in the desert.

Text 2: A hospital safety report found that new nurses who hesitated to ask questions made more medication errors in their first year than those who asked often.

Which theme do the texts share?
options: Pride and fear can be fatal for wild birds.
New nurses make many errors in their first year.
Refusing to ask for help can lead to harm.
Experienced workers should train new staff.
C.why: The crow's pride and the new nurses' hesitation both keep them from asking for help, and both lead to harm. That shared message fits a fable and a safety report alike.

whyNot.0: This fits only the fable and narrows it to birds.
whyNot.1: This is a detail from Text 2, and the report compares nurses who asked with those who did not.
whyNot.3: Neither text recommends training; this adds a recommendation.

reteach.title: Think of two songs about the same feeling
reteach.question: A slow country ballad and an upbeat pop song can both be about moving on after a breakup. How can two very different songs share one message?

blocks.body: The ballad might tell one woman's story with sad guitar; the pop song might shout about dancing it off. The style, speed and mood differ, but both say the same thing about life: you can heal and move forward. Texts work the same way. A poem and a news report can share a theme even though one is emotional and one is factual. Look past the style to the message.

blocks.text: 'Breakups' is the topic of both songs, not the theme. The theme is what the songs say ABOUT breakups, as a full sentence.

explain.body: A topic is a word or phrase (loyalty). A theme is a complete statement about life (Loyalty is tested in hard times). If an answer has no verb or claim, it is a topic.

rows.label: Example
values: Loyalty is tested in hard times

test.q: A short story follows a teenager who lies to her friends to seem popular and ends up losing their trust. Which choice is a THEME rather than a topic?
options: Friendship and honesty among teenage girls
Dishonesty can destroy the trust it seeks to win.
A teenager lies to her friends and loses them.
Popularity and peer pressure in high school
test.why: This is a complete, general statement about life drawn from the story: the lies meant to win friends cost her their trust.

whyNot.0: This names the subject with no message, so it is a topic.
whyNot.2: This summarizes the plot of one story; a theme is a general lesson.
whyNot.3: This is a topic phrase with no claim.

explain.body: A plot summary retells what happens to particular characters. A theme lifts the lesson out of the story so it applies to people in general. Drop the names and events, keep the insight.

test.q:
Read the passage.

When the café owner offered Rafael double pay to keep quiet about the expired milk, he refused and reported it to the health department. He lost the job, but two weeks later the inspector who handled the case recommended him for a position at the county.

Which statement best expresses the theme?
options: Rafael reports a café and later finds a county job.
Health inspectors check cafés for expired products.
Doing the right thing can be costly but rewarding.
Café owners often break health rules to save money.
test.why: Rafael's honesty costs him his job but leads to a better one. The general lesson is that doing the right thing can carry a cost and a reward.

whyNot.0: This is a plot summary tied to one character.
whyNot.1: This is a fact about the topic, not a message about life.
whyNot.3: This generalizes about café owners from one example; it is not the story's lesson.

explain.body: When a question asks what BOTH texts express, test each option against each text separately. An option that fits one text perfectly but not the other is the classic trap.

test.q:
Read the two texts.

Text 1: After her stroke, Doris relearned to write her name one letter a day.

Text 2: A physical therapist explains that patients who set small daily goals often regain function faster than those who aim only for full recovery.

Which idea is expressed in BOTH texts?
options: Strokes mostly affect a person's ability to write.
Physical therapists set goals for their patients.
Full recovery should be every patient's goal.
Small daily steps can support a long recovery.
test.why: Doris's letter-a-day progress and the therapist's advice about small daily goals both show small steps supporting recovery.

whyNot.0: Text 1 mentions writing, but neither text claims this about strokes in general.
whyNot.1: This fits only Text 2, and in Text 2 it is the patients who set goals.
whyNot.2: Text 2 suggests small goals work better than aiming only for full recovery.

explain.body: Two texts can share a theme yet differ in genre (poem vs article), purpose (to express vs to inform), tone (emotional vs neutral) or evidence (one person's story vs data). Contrast questions ask about these differences.

test.q:
Read the two texts.

Text 1 (diary): Day 30 without soda. I miss the fizz, but I sleep through the night now, and I don't crash at 3 p.m.

Text 2 (fact sheet): Cutting back on sugary drinks is linked to steadier energy and better sleep in many adults.

Which statement best contrasts the two texts?
options: Text 1 opposes soda; Text 2 says soda is healthy.
Text 1 is one experience; Text 2 is a general claim.
Text 1 is about energy; Text 2 is about weight loss.
Text 1 states a fact; Text 2 gives a personal opinion.
test.why: Both connect cutting sugary drinks to better sleep and energy. The diary reports one person's experience; the fact sheet makes a general claim about many adults.

whyNot.0: Both texts favor cutting back; they do not disagree.
whyNot.2: Text 2 discusses energy and sleep, not weight loss.
whyNot.3: This reverses them: the diary is the personal account, and the fact sheet makes a general, impersonal claim.
